transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from the NPR News
in Washington, I'm Windsor
Johnston.
A leadership contest is taking
shape among Senate Democrats
as the party prepares
to retake control
of the chamber in January.
Maryland Senator Chris Van
Holland says he'll challenge
longtime Democratic leader
Chuck Schumer for the top job.
NPR's Luke Garrett reports
the winner would become
Senate Majority Leader helping
shape the party's agenda
for the next two years.
>> In a statement, Senator Van
Holland said Americans called
for change at the ballot box,
and that means new leadership
in the Senate.
Senator-elect Abdul Sayed told
NPR he supports Van Holland,
citing his "righteous fights
against the Trump
administration."
Schumer does maintain support
within his caucus.
Senator Angus King,
an independent from Maine who
votes with Democrats, endorsed
Schumer and called him
the architect of the most
successful election
in modern history.
Democratic Senate leadership
elections are set
for early December.
Luke Garrett, NPR News,
Washington.
>> As Democrats prepared
to retake control of Congress
in January, voter turnout
in the midterm elections
was historically high,
as NPR's Domenico
Montanaro reports.
>> Turnout in this election
was almost a record.
According to the University
of Florida Election Lab,
which tracks turnout,
49.1% of eligible voters
cast ballots across the country
in this year's midterm elections.
That's just a tick lower
than the 50% who showed up
to vote in 2018,
which was the highest mark
in more than 100 years.
The states that saw the highest
turnout were Maine,
Michigan, and Minnesota.
The lowest were Arkansas,
Oklahoma, and Tennessee.
The overall turnout
in this election represented
a trend during the Trump era
of higher-than-usual
midterm participation.
But it was still 24% lower
than the 2024 presidential
election.
Domenico Montanaro, NPR News,
Washington.
>> The federal government's new
fiscal year is starting out
much like the old one,
deep in the red.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports
on the government's more
than $400 billion deficit
in the month of October.
>> Setting aside some calendar
quirks, government tax receipts
were down 6% in October,
compared to a year ago,
while government spending was up
by 12%.
Some of that spending increase
just reflects a return
to normal operations,
compared to October 2025,
when the government was shut
down.
The Agriculture Department also
spent an extra $14 billion
last month, with much of that
going to help farmers who were
hard-hit by the president's
trade policies and the high cost
associated with the war
with Iran.
In addition, the government
paid $115 billion
in interest last month,
an 11% increase from October
of 2025.
Borrowing costs have been
climbing as a result
of higher interest rates
and the government's
ballooning debt.
Scott Horsley, NPR News,
Washington.
>> Microsoft says it's
gradually restoring services
following a worldwide outage.
The company reports improved
email access, though some users
may still experience problems.
This is "NPR News."
SpaceX says it's preparing
another test launch of its
massive Starship rocket.
NPR's Jeff Rumfield reports,
some worry it may be leaving
behind a key partner.
>> Starship is the largest
rocket ever built.
It's super powerful.
>> Three, two, one.
>> But it can't carry humans
into orbit.
That job falls to a much
smaller rocket called Falcon 9,
which SpaceX now plans
to retire.
Falcon 9 has been a workhorse
for NASA, which uses it to
reach the International Space
Station, but Tim Ferrar
with TMF Associates says
SpaceX isn't earning enough
from launching astronauts.
>> It's not making a lot of
money out of NASA,
although it seems likely
that the individual missions
are profitable.
They're small potatoes.
>> Ferrar says NASA contracts
save SpaceX from bankruptcy
over a decade ago, but today,
the company sees more profit
from satellite Internet
and eventually data centers
in space.
Jeff Brumfield, NPR News.
>> European Union leaders
are gathering in Dublin today
for their first summit focused
on artificial intelligence.
The talks will examine how
Europe can strengthen its
position against the United
States and China.
Leaders will discuss
investment, energy supplies,
and infrastructure needed
to expand the technology.
The agenda also includes
AI's effects on jobs,
children's rights,
and democratic institutions.
Stocks across Asia traded
mixed today, with Japan's
Nikkei average of more
than 300 points on Wall Street
down futures are trading
higher at this hour.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Maryland Senator Chris Van Holland announces challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader
Senator Angus King endorses Schumer, backed by Abdul Sayed supporting Van Holland
US midterm voter turnout nears record at 49.1 percent, lower than 2024 presidential election
Government deficit exceeds $400 billion in October as spending rises and tax receipts fall
Microsoft gradually restoring services after worldwide outage, with some email problems persisting
SpaceX preparing another Starship test launch and plans to retire Falcon 9 rocket
European Union leaders gather in Dublin for first summit focused on artificial intelligence
Asian stocks trade mixed while Japan's Nikkei falls over 300 points
